items.prompt: A parts catalog receives exact SKU queries such as AX-4407 and natural-language requests such as “a corrosion-resistant coupling for an outdoor line.” Which retrieval strategy should serve both patterns?
constraints: Exact identifiers need location fidelity.
Paraphrased descriptions need semantic matching, while catalog filters must constrain the candidate set.

options.text: Use embeddings alone for every query and rely on semantic similarity to preserve exact SKU spelling and catalog filters.
Combine lexical and semantic candidates, apply structured catalog filters, and rerank or merge the resulting set for the query type.
Use lexical-only matching for every query, relying on exact terms and catalog metadata even when a natural-language description uses different words.
Use semantic embeddings for every query and apply catalog filters only after the top-K candidates are returned, then let Claude choose among them.

feedback.Reason: Exact SKU and natural-language retrieval have different signals. Lexical search preserves identifiers, semantic search handles paraphrases, and structured filters keep the combined candidates valid.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A hybrid retriever builds candidate sets from lexical and embedding signals, applies metadata or field filters, and reranks using the query and catalog relevance.
Details.scenarioApplication: Match AX-4407 lexically, search description concepts semantically, filter by product status and dimensions, and return cited candidates with the selection reason.
Details.errorCorrection: Choose retrieval signals from query shape rather than adopting embeddings or recency as a universal relevance rule.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Hybrid retrieval requires two indexes and merge tuning, but it avoids exact-match misses and semantic drift while retaining catalog constraints.
Details.transfer: For mixed identifier and descriptive queries, combine lexical and semantic retrieval and evaluate filters and ranking on both query slices.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: Embeddings can miss exact identifiers or blur SKU variants, and they do not automatically enforce structured catalog constraints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Lexical-only matching protects exact terms but can miss paraphrased descriptions such as corrosion resistance or outdoor use.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Semantic candidates can lose exact SKU fidelity, and filtering only after top-K can exclude a valid part before the catalog constraints are applied.

items.prompt: A monitoring assistant answers a “latest completed-release p95” question from vectorized narrative reports and sometimes cites an older release, even though a time-series database has the current metric. What retrieval diagnosis is correct?
constraints: The requested value is structured, current, and keyed by release and time.
Narrative reports may explain the value but are not the numeric system of record.

options.text: Increase vector top-K and ask Claude to compare all returned release narratives before selecting the latest p95.
Re-embed the metric name and remove release filters so semantic similarity can identify the newest value from the entire narrative corpus.
Route the value lookup to the metrics API with explicit release and time filters, then retrieve narrative context only to explain or cite the result.
Keep the narrative retriever authoritative and add a sentence asking Claude to prefer dates that look recent in the retrieved passages.

feedback.Reason: A latest metric is a structured lookup with explicit keys. Vector narrative search can supply explanatory context after the authoritative value is obtained, but increasing semantic search cannot make it complete or current.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The metrics API applies time and release predicates and returns the value; narrative retrieval is a secondary explanation source with its own citation boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: Query the completed-release series for p95, join the release ID to narrative notes, and show both numeric provenance and explanatory passages.
Details.errorCorrection: Route each query to the source and retrieval signal that matches its data shape instead of tuning the wrong retriever.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Two retrieval paths require routing and source reconciliation, but they prevent stale narrative values from masquerading as current metrics.
Details.transfer: For current aggregates or time-series values, use a structured source of record and retrieve prose only for context or causal explanation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: More narrative candidates increase stale evidence and do not establish complete release and time filtering.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: Removing release filters widens the stale candidate set and re-embedding cannot make prose authoritative for a structured metric.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: A wording instruction cannot reliably select the current value from incomplete or differently scoped narratives.

items.prompt: A versioned maintenance manual has product and section metadata plus thousands of semantically related passages. A technician asks about a product generation and symptom. Which retrieval boundary should be applied first?
constraints: Product generation and active manual version constrain the candidate universe.
Semantic ranking is needed for varied symptom language after metadata filtering.

options.text: Filter by product generation and active manual version first, then run semantic retrieval and reranking within the remaining sections.
Search every manual version semantically and ask Claude to infer which generation the technician probably means from the top passages.
Use section titles as the only retrieval signal so the assistant never has to compare symptom language.
Embed each complete manual as one document and return the whole top manual for the technician to scan.

feedback.Reason: Metadata is authoritative for product and version scope; semantic retrieval then handles the varied symptom wording within that constrained set.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Structured filters narrow candidates before embedding or reranker scoring, reducing cross-version contamination while preserving semantic recall.
Details.scenarioApplication: Require a product generation and active-version filter, retrieve symptom-related sections, and cite the manual revision and section in the answer.
Details.errorCorrection: Apply deterministic candidate boundaries before semantic relevance when metadata defines the correct corpus slice.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Missing or unreliable metadata can reduce recall, so the service needs a validation or uncertainty path rather than silently searching every version.
Details.transfer: For versioned documentation, filter by authoritative metadata first and use semantic ranking inside the valid candidate universe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: Searching every version allows stale or wrong-generation evidence to rank and asks generation to infer an authoritative scope.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Titles alone discard symptom synonyms and details needed for the technician's question.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Whole-manual retrieval loses section precision and floods context with unrelated generations or procedures.

items.prompt: A code assistant searches a large monorepo. Developers use exact symbol names and file paths for navigation, then ask conceptual questions about request flow. Which TWO retrieval choices fit? Select TWO.
constraints: Exact navigation needs lexical location fidelity.
Conceptual explanation should load connected detail only after an initial match.

options.text: Use semantic retrieval over repository files for symbols and concepts in one pass, accepting that exact symbol collisions and file locations are resolved after retrieval.
Use lexical or indexed symbol and path search first, then hydrate connected files and call sites just in time for a conceptual explanation.
Use filename and path substring search to return candidate files, but do not hydrate definitions, callers, or connected files for the conceptual explanation.
Use curated architecture documentation for both symbol-navigation and request-flow questions, returning documentation section links instead of exact code locations.
Preserve symbol and path identifiers in the retrieved evidence so the explanation can cite exact locations and scope its expansion.

feedback.Reason: Lexical indexes preserve exact code locations, while just-in-time expansion supplies enough connected context for conceptual reasoning. Identifiers keep that expansion auditable and focused.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An initial symbol/path lookup returns lightweight references; the retriever loads callers, definitions, or connected files only when the conceptual question requires them.
Details.scenarioApplication: Resolve `handleRequest` and its path first, load the relevant handler and call sites, and cite file and line identifiers in the explanation.
Details.errorCorrection: Separate navigation retrieval from conceptual hydration and preserve source addresses instead of dumping the repository into context.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The assistant may need another retrieval call, but it avoids context overload and improves location fidelity and citation.
Details.transfer: For source-code retrieval, use exact indexes for navigation and bounded just-in-time expansion for broader architectural explanations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: Semantic file retrieval can blur exact symbol collisions and does not preserve the location fidelity needed for navigation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Path matching can find candidates but without connected definitions and callers it cannot explain the request flow or provide sufficient evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Architecture documentation can explain intended flow, but its section links do not resolve exact symbols and paths or supply the connected implementation evidence required here.

omittedCorrectElementExplanationsByOptio.b: Without an exact initial lookup and just-in-time expansion, navigation and conceptual explanation compete for an oversized context.
omittedCorrectElementExplanationsByOptio.e: Without preserved symbol and path identifiers, the expanded explanation cannot reliably cite or constrain its source locations.

items.prompt: A finance user asks for total refunds, median amount, and week-over-week change by region. Refund records are authoritative in a warehouse; vectorized policy notes explain refund reasons. Which data path should answer?
constraints: Complete current aggregates need explicit time, region, and tenant filters.
Policy prose is supplementary explanation, not the arithmetic source.

options.text: Embed every refund record and ask Claude to sum, rank, and compare the nearest chunks, treating semantic coverage as the aggregate membership rule.
Use vectorized policy notes as the primary source and infer regional totals from examples and reason frequencies contained in those notes.
Execute the aggregate in the warehouse with explicit time, region, and tenant filters, then retrieve policy notes only to explain the result.
Return the newest refund records as a sample and have Claude estimate the median and week-over-week change from that subset.

feedback.Reason: The warehouse can compute complete, current aggregates with explicit filters. Vector notes add reason context but cannot guarantee membership, freshness, or arithmetic across all refunds.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Structured aggregation performs the numeric operation and returns its query scope; semantic retrieval supplements it with cited policy explanations.
Details.scenarioApplication: Run total, median, and change grouped by region and tenant, then retrieve the relevant refund-policy sections for the narrative.
Details.errorCorrection: Route complete quantitative questions to the structured system of record and reserve semantic retrieval for representative explanation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The answer needs two sources and a join, but it avoids an unbounded vector sum and makes filters auditable.
Details.transfer: For current aggregates, preserve completeness and arithmetic in the structured source and retrieve prose only for causal or policy context.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: Nearest chunks do not guarantee all refunds or correct arithmetic and can omit records outside semantic similarity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: Policy examples are not a complete transactional dataset and cannot establish current regional totals or medians.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: A recent sample cannot produce a complete total, median, or week-over-week comparison for the requested scope.

items.prompt: An HR assistant must answer who reports to a manager and whether a transfer is permitted. The authoritative data is a versioned relationship graph with effective dates and access controls; handbook prose is supplementary. Which retrieval path is correct?
constraints: Current relationship and authorization facts require an authorized structured source.
Handbook text can explain the policy after the current facts are retrieved.

options.text: Query the authorized relationship source for the chain and effective-date decision, then retrieve handbook sections to explain the policy.
Search handbook embeddings for names and ask Claude to infer the reporting chain and transfer permission from similar passages.
Use the newest handbook paragraph as the authority and ask a manager to correct any relationship detail after the response.
Return all graph and handbook records to Claude so it can reconcile effective dates and access scope in one context.

feedback.Reason: The graph contains current relationship and access facts, so it must answer those questions. Handbook retrieval can explain policy but cannot establish live membership or enforce access.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Authorized structured queries apply effective-date and tenant predicates; semantic handbook retrieval supplies scoped explanatory text after the fact lookup.
Details.scenarioApplication: Check the requester's scope, query the current reporting chain and transfer rule, then cite the applicable handbook section without exposing unauthorized records.
Details.errorCorrection: Use the authoritative structured source for mutable relationships and permissions, not a semantically similar policy passage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The assistant needs routing and access checks across two sources, but it avoids stale inferences and keeps sensitive graph data controlled.
Details.transfer: For organizational or authorization facts, query the current structured relationship source first and use prose only to explain the resulting policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: Similar handbook prose may be stale or incomplete and cannot enforce the current graph relationship or requester access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: A handbook paragraph does not establish live reporting membership, and post-response correction is too late for a sensitive answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: Dumping all records exposes data and leaves effective dates, access scope, and source authority for generation to infer.

items.prompt: A retrieval service must answer whether an EU invoice may be retained 90 days. The top result says the global policy allows 30 days; an active EU appendix allows 90 days only for a legal hold, but the retrieved chunk omits the invoice's hold status. Claude drafts 90 days citing the appendix. What should the service do?
constraints: The answer depends on a missing legal-hold variable and conflicting scoped evidence.
Similarity rank alone cannot resolve the conflict.

options.text: Raise top-K and select the highest-scoring clause, assuming the EU appendix controls because it is more specific than the global policy.
Ask Claude to reconcile both passages in prose and publish the answer with both citations even though the legal-hold status is missing.
Discard the global policy as less relevant and return 90 days whenever any active EU appendix appears in the result set.
Mark the evidence contradictory or insufficient, perform one bounded metadata or full-document check, and answer only if hold status resolves; otherwise abstain or escalate with both references.

feedback.Reason: The controlling condition is missing, so ranking or model reconciliation cannot establish a safe retention period. A bounded evidence check can resolve the hold state; otherwise the service must expose uncertainty.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Retrieval settings can broaden inclusion but do not create the missing scope fact; metadata or full-document inspection supplies the decisive variable before generation.
Details.scenarioApplication: Check the invoice hold status and active policy scope, cite the 90-day appendix only when held, or return the 30-day global rule/uncertainty path with both references.
Details.errorCorrection: Treat conflicting retrieval as an evidence diagnosis and require the missing condition before converting passages into a confident answer.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The answer may be delayed or escalated, but that is safer than turning a high-scoring incomplete passage into a retention decision.
Details.transfer: When retrieved evidence conflicts and a material scope variable is absent, perform bounded verification and make unresolved state explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: More candidates and specificity do not resolve the missing hold status and can make confidence depend on rank.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: Prose reconciliation cannot invent the absent condition and may publish a different answer on another run.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: EU scope alone is insufficient; the appendix's 90-day rule is conditional and the global policy remains relevant when no hold exists.

items.prompt:
A warehouse operator asks for one exact current SKU, AX-4407, and the catalog contains a single authoritative row with that identifier. There are no synonyms, paraphrase needs, or missing fields; a lexical key lookup returns the row in 20 ms.

Which retrieval path is proportionate to this exact, authoritative key lookup?
constraints: The request contains one exact current SKU and the catalog has a single authoritative row with no missing fields or synonyms.
Lexical lookup returns the row in 20 ms; semantic search returns 20 discontinued near-matches in 180 ms.
Tenant and active-version filters are enforced by the structured source.

options.text: Use a filtered lexical-and-semantic search for the SKU so the same retrieval path can handle future natural-language requests.
Search the semantic index first and fall back to the exact key only when the top result is not confident.
Use an unfiltered string match across the catalog because the SKU is unique in the global dataset.
Use filtered exact-key lookup; add semantic retrieval only for a separately evidenced natural-language need.

feedback.Reason: The source and query shape are exact and complete, so semantic similarity adds latency and ambiguity without improving recall.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RAG systems should choose a source and retrieval approach that matches the information need; lexical BM25 and embeddings provide different signals. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: When the information need is one exact authoritative identifier, lexical or key lookup is sufficient and safer than adding semantic retrieval.
Details.scenarioApplication: Use an exact lexical/key lookup with tenant and active-version filters, and expose semantic retrieval only for a separately evidenced natural-language need.
Details.errorCorrection: The semantic candidate set adds discontinued near-matches and latency to a query whose authoritative key already resolves uniquely.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the operator asks for a descriptive alternative or the key is absent, add semantic candidates and evaluate the hybrid route on that changed need.
Details.transfer: Route each information need through the smallest governed interface that matches its evidence shape, and preserve explicit authorization, freshness, and unavailable states when the evidence cannot support a claim.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a: The request is an exact authoritative key lookup; adding semantic retrieval for possible future wording introduces discontinued near-matches and latency without an evidenced need.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: The exact key is already authoritative and complete; making a noisy semantic ranking the first gate adds ambiguity and delay.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Global uniqueness does not establish the caller's tenant or active revision; the structured lookup must enforce both filters.

items.prompt:
An incident analyst asks for the latest seven-day error rate and a short explanation from 500,000 log narratives. The metrics table is authoritative and updates every hour; only three relevant narrative excerpts fit the 4,000-token context budget.

Which source and loading order should answer both the metric and its explanation?
constraints: The hourly metrics table is authoritative for the latest seven-day error rate.
The narrative corpus has 500,000 tokens and only three relevant excerpts fit the 4,000-token context.
The service and time window become available after the filtered aggregate and can narrow just-in-time retrieval.

options.text: Query the filtered metrics aggregate first, then retrieve up to three current narratives just in time and label the sources.
Send all 500,000 log narratives to semantic retrieval and let the top paragraph answer both the metric and explanation.
Retrieve three narratives first and infer the seven-day error rate from their language before checking the metrics table.
Use the metrics table only and omit narrative retrieval because the numeric aggregate is sufficient for the user.

feedback.Reason: The decision combines source-specific retrieval with token-aware JIT detail, preserving both numeric freshness and explanatory context.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Just-in-time retrieval uses lightweight identifiers to load detailed information only when relevant, keeping context focused. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Route the query according to source shape and use the context budget to load explanation evidence only after the structured result narrows the search.
Details.scenarioApplication: Query the metrics source for the filtered aggregate, then use the service and time window to retrieve up to three current narrative excerpts just in time; label the metric and explanation separately.
Details.errorCorrection: The narrative index can return stale similar incidents, and the full corpus cannot fit the request; the metric must come from the structured source.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the metrics table is unavailable, expose the error rate as unavailable and retrieve narratives only as qualitative context, without fabricating a numeric answer.
Details.transfer: Route each information need through the smallest governed interface that matches its evidence shape, and preserve explicit authorization, freshness, and unavailable states when the evidence cannot support a claim.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.b: The narrative index can return stale similar incidents, and the full corpus cannot fit the request; the metric must come from the structured source.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c: Narrative excerpts cannot establish the authoritative aggregate; the metric must narrow the explanation search rather than follow it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.d: The metric is authoritative for the number, but the request also asks for a short explanation that needs bounded, current narrative evidence.
